explanation: Kneading lines gluten strands up into an elastic web that traps gas from the yeast. Rye flour forms a weak gluten network and rice flour none, so their breads rise less.

claims.text: Gluten, formed from wheat proteins when flour is mixed with water, gives bread dough its elasticity.
Casein is a milk protein, collagen an animal connective-tissue protein and albumin a protein of egg white and blood; none forms the stretchy network of bread dough.
Kneading develops gluten into an elastic network that traps the gas produced by yeast.
Rye and rice flours form little or no gluten, so breads made from them rise less than wheat breads.

evidence.restatement: When wheat flour is wetted, gliadin and glutenin form gluten, the elastic network that lets dough stretch.
Casein is the main milk protein, collagen the connective-tissue protein and albumin the protein of egg white and blood plasma; none forms the dough network.
Kneading develops the gluten network, which traps the carbon dioxide made by yeast.
Rye and rice flours form little or no gluten network, so breads made from them rise less than wheat bread.
Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin are hydrated and worked, and it gives dough its elasticity.
Casein is the main milk protein, albumin the protein of egg white and blood, collagen the connective tissue protein; none forms the dough network.
Kneading aligns the gluten into an elastic web that traps the carbon dioxide yeast produces.
Rice flour has no gluten. Rye flour has gluten-type proteins but forms only a weak network, so rye and rice breads rise less than wheat bread.

claimResults.note: Rye does contain gluten proteins (secalin) and is not safe in coeliac disease. 'Little or no' is defensible because rye's network is weak, but see the wording note.

issues.note: c4: rye flour does contain gluten-forming proteins and is off limits in coeliac disease. 'Little or no' is defensible because rye forms a weak network, yet a reader could take it as rye being low in gluten. Consider 'rice flour, which has none, and rye, whose gluten network is weak'.
